nodes.label: Displacement
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Displacement is the vector quantity representing change in position of an object from initial to final point, including both magnitude and direction. Unlike distance (scalar), displacement can be zero even if the object has moved, if it returns to its starting point. It is the foundational vector in all of kinematics.

nodes.label: Velocity
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time — a vector quantity with both magnitude (speed) and direction. Average velocity = Δx/Δt. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative dx/dt. A common misconception is conflating speed (scalar) with velocity (vector) — an object moving in a circle at constant speed has changing velocity because direction changes.

nodes.label: Acceleration
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time. It is a vector — it has magnitude and direction. Crucially, an object can be accelerating even at constant speed if its direction changes (centripetal acceleration). Free-fall acceleration near Earth's surface is g = 9.8 m/s² downward, regardless of mass.

nodes.label: Newton's Laws of Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Newton's three laws: (1) An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force — inertia. (2) Net force equals mass times acceleration: F = ma. (3) For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A critical misconception is that heavier objects fall faster — in reality free-fall acceleration is independent of mass (ignoring air resistance).

nodes.label: Momentum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity: p = mv. It is a vector quantity. The net force on a system equals the rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt — this is actually the more general form of Newton's second law. In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum is conserved.

nodes.label: Impulse
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Impulse is the change in momentum of an object: J = Δp = F·Δt. It equals force multiplied by the time interval over which it acts. The impulse-momentum theorem states that the impulse on an object equals its change in momentum. This is why airbags reduce injury — they increase the time of impact, reducing peak force.

nodes.label: Conservation of Momentum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: In an isolated system where no external forces act, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. p_initial = p_final. This applies to all collisions and explosions. Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy. Inelastic collisions conserve only momentum.

nodes.label: Projectile Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Projectile motion describes objects launched into the air subject only to gravity. Horizontal and vertical components are independent — horizontal velocity is constant, vertical velocity changes at g = 9.8 m/s². The trajectory is parabolic. Maximum range for a given speed occurs at 45°. A critical insight: a horizontally thrown ball and a dropped ball hit the ground at the same time.

nodes.label: Circular Motion
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Circular motion requires centripetal acceleration directed toward the center: a = v²/r. The centripetal force is not a separate force — it is the net inward force provided by existing forces (gravity, tension, normal force). A common misconception is believing centrifugal force pushes outward — in an inertial frame, no outward force exists; the object simply resists direction change due to inertia.

nodes.label: Work and Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Work is done when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force: W = F·d·cosθ. The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE. Energy is the capacity to do work. Power is the rate of work done: P = W/t.

nodes.label: Kinetic Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion: KE = ½mv². It is always positive (scalar), proportional to the square of velocity, and proportional to mass. Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy. The work-energy theorem directly connects net work to change in KE.

nodes.label: Potential Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Potential energy is stored energy due to position or configuration. Gravitational PE: PE = mgh (near Earth's surface). Elastic PE: PE = ½kx² (spring). It is energy that has the potential to become kinetic. The zero reference point for PE is arbitrary — only changes in PE matter physically.

nodes.label: Conservation of Energy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: The total energy of an isolated system remains constant — energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted between forms. KE + PE = constant (in the absence of non-conservative forces). With friction, mechanical energy is converted to thermal energy but total energy is still conserved. This is one of the most fundamental laws in all of physics.
aliases: energy cannot be created or destroyed

nodes.label: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not — some is converted to heat, sound, or deformation. A perfectly inelastic collision is one where the objects stick together. Real-world collisions are nearly always inelastic.

nodes.label: Gravitation
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Newton's law of universal gravitation: every mass attracts every other mass with force F = Gm₁m₂/r². The gravitational field strength g near Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s². Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces but has infinite range. It governs planetary orbits, tides, and the structure of the universe.

nodes.label: Orbital Mechanics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Kepler's three laws govern orbital motion: (1) Orbits are ellipses with the star at one focus. (2) A planet sweeps equal areas in equal times — meaning it moves faster at perihelion and slower at aphelion. (3) T² ∝ a³ (orbital period squared proportional to semi-major axis cubed). A common misconception is that orbits are circular — in reality all natural orbits are ellipses.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Angular momentum L = Iω = r × p is a vector quantity conserved in the absence of external torques. It explains why a spinning skater speeds up when pulling in their arms (reduced I → increased ω to conserve L). Torque τ = dL/dt. For a point mass orbiting: L = mvr. Conservation of angular momentum is why planets speed up near the sun.
aliases: moment of inertia times angular velocity

nodes.label: Electric Charge
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter. Charges are positive or negative; like charges repel, unlike charges attract. The unit is the coulomb (C). Charge is quantised in units of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Charge is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Conductors allow charge flow; insulators resist it.

nodes.label: Coulomb's Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Coulomb's law describes the electrostatic force between two point charges: F = kq₁q₂/r². This has the same form as Newton's gravitational law but can be repulsive (for like charges) unlike gravity. k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The force is along the line joining the charges.

nodes.label: Electric Field
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: An electric field E is the force per unit charge at a point in space: E = F/q. Field lines run from positive to negative charges. A uniform electric field between parallel plates: E = V/d. The field concept allows us to describe how charges affect space around them before another charge is placed there.

nodes.label: Electric Potential and Voltage
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Electric potential V is the potential energy per unit charge at a point: V = U/q (volts). Voltage (potential difference) is the work done per unit charge moving a charge between two points: V = W/q. A critical insight: charges flow from high to low potential (current flows from + to −). V is a scalar, E is a vector — they are related by E = −dV/dx.

nodes.label: Electric Circuits
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Ohm's law: V = IR (voltage equals current times resistance). Kirchhoff's laws: (1) Current law — sum of currents into a node = 0. (2) Voltage law — sum of voltages around a loop = 0. Series: same current, voltages add. Parallel: same voltage, currents add. Power dissipated: P = IV = I²R = V²/R.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic Induction
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Faraday's law: a changing magnetic flux induces an EMF: ε = −dΦ/dt. Lenz's law states the induced current opposes the change causing it (negative sign). This is the principle behind generators, transformers, and electric motors. A conductor moving through a magnetic field or a changing B field both induce EMF.

nodes.label: Maxwell's Equations
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Maxwell's four equations unify electricity and magnetism and predict electromagnetic waves. (1) Gauss's law for E: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀. (2) Gauss's law for B: ∇·B = 0 (no magnetic monopoles). (3) Faraday's law: ∇×E = −∂B/∂t. (4) Ampere-Maxwell law: ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t. The displacement current term (∂E/∂t) was Maxwell's key addition, predicting light as an EM wave at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).

nodes.label: Temperature and Thermal Equilibrium
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. The zeroth law of thermodynamics: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other — this defines temperature as a measurable quantity. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat flow between objects.

nodes.label: First Law of Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: The first law is conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems: ΔU = Q − W. The internal energy change of a system equals heat added minus work done by the system. Heat and work are both energy in transit. This means you cannot build a perpetual motion machine of the first kind — you cannot extract more energy than you put in.

nodes.label: Second Law of Thermodynamics
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: The second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system can only increase over time. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never in reverse without external work. No heat engine can be 100% efficient (Carnot efficiency: η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot). This law introduces the arrow of time and explains why processes are irreversible.

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: Entropy S is a measure of the disorder or number of microstates of a system. Boltzmann's formula: S = k_B·ln(W) where W is the number of microstates. Entropy always increases in spontaneous processes in isolated systems. A common misconception is that entropy means energy is lost — it means energy becomes less available to do useful work.

nodes.label: Ideal Gas Law
nodes.subject: physics
nodes.description: The ideal gas law: PV = nRT (P=pressure, V=volume, n=moles, R=8.314 J/mol·K, T=temperature in Kelvin). For a fixed amount of gas: Boyle's law (PV = const at fixed T), Charles's law (V/T = const at fixed P), Gay-Lussac's law (P/T = const at fixed V). An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces and negligible particle volume.
